newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish Islamists challenge secular government.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Islamists challenge secular government.

text.p: Turkey's new government faced a challenge to its secularist rule on Wednesday after thousands of angry Islamists marched through the capital demanding an end to plans to curtail religious education.

But Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz, brought to power on the back of a secularist backlash against the previous Islamist-led government, vowed to push on with the plans, which put secularists and Islamists on a collision course.
The government plans to extend compulsory education to eight years from the present five, effectively closing many religious schools known as Imam Hatips.
Secularist education reform was a key demand by the army in an anti-Islamist campaign dating back to February that helped topple the previous government of Necmettin Erbakan.
Thousands of Islamists took their discontent to the streets on Tuesday, marching through the centre of the capital.
Police used batons, dogs and water cannon to break up the protest and prevent marchers reaching key government buildings.
Dozens of police in full riot gear, some with dogs, charged a group of about 1,000 protesters marching towards Yilmaz's office chanting: "Government, resign!"
"Break the hands of those who try to lay a finger on the Koran," they shouted, referring to the Moslem holy book.
The police also beat reporters and cameramen covering the demonstration, injuring five and drawing heavy criticism from politicians and human rights groups.
The demonstrators' chanting could be heard inside the headquarters of Turkey's secularist military where the top brass were briefing key cabinet members on the dangers of Islamist activism.
The armed forces fear that Islamic activism is on the rise and in February put forward a package of anti-Islamist measures.
Erbakan, then in power, did little to implement them.
But new prime minister Yilmaz has said he will push the reform through parliament by the end of next week despite opposition from at least 10 pro-Islamist MPs within his Motherland Party.
Yilmaz's loose right-left coalition won a vote of confidence with a slim 25-seat majority earlier this month.
Erbakan's Welfare Party is resolutely opposed to the plan, saying it is an attack on religious freedom.
"Their only goal is to see who can close the most Imam Hatips, Koranic courses and charities," Erbakan, now the main opposition leader, told his Welfare deputies.

Firebrand Islamist deputy Hasan Huseyin Ceylan was hoisted aloft by the Ankara crowd, many of whom were bearded and wore Islamic-style skullcaps. One group of protesters was invited into parliament by Welfare MPs to hear Erbakan.
